items.title: Seeking Wealth Rightly, and Using It Without Being Bound by It

items.zh: 如理作意相應尋伺求者，謂如有一，不以非法及不兇險追求財物。
items.en: As for the seeking of applied and sustained thought associated with sound reasoning attention: it is as when someone seeks wealth by lawful and blameless means, rather than by unlawful and blameworthy means.

items.zh: 如理作意相應尋伺受用者，謂如即彼追求財已，不染、不住、不耽、不縛、不悶、不著、亦不堅執，深見過患，了知出離而受用之。
items.en: As for the enjoyment of applied and sustained thought associated with sound reasoning attention: it is as when that same person, having sought and obtained wealth, makes use of it without defiling attachment, without hoarding, without craving indulgence, without being bound by it, without being confounded by it, without clinging to it, and without stubbornly grasping it — seeing deeply into its dangers, and making use of it with a clear understanding of how to be free of it.

items.title: Correct Conduct: Honouring Elders, Fearing Wrongdoing, Practising Generosity

items.zh: 如理作意相應尋伺正行者，謂如有一，了知父母、沙門、婆羅門，及家長等，恭敬供養，利益承事。於今世後世所作罪中，見大怖畏；行施作福，受齋持戒。
items.en: As for the correct conduct of applied and sustained thought associated with sound reasoning attention: it is as when someone, recognising their parents, renunciants, learned teachers, and family elders as deserving of it, reveres, provides for, benefits, and attends upon them; regards any wrongdoing committed in this present life or the next with profound dread; and practices generosity, cultivates merit, observes the one-day eight-precept fast, and upholds the precepts.

items.title: Three Vehicles, Three Provisions — Promised in Full Much Later

items.zh: 聲聞乘資糧方便者，聲聞地中我當廣說。獨覺乘資糧方便者，獨覺地中我當廣說。波羅蜜多引發方便者，菩薩地中我當廣說。
items.en: As for the means of provisioning the śrāvaka vehicle: this I shall explain fully in the Śrāvaka Stage. As for the means of provisioning the pratyekabuddha vehicle: this I shall explain fully in the Pratyekabuddha Stage. As for the means of drawing forth the perfections: this I shall explain fully in the Bodhisattva Stage.

items.title: A Detailed Elaboration Begins: the Four Marks of a True Almsgiver

items.zh: 復次，施主有四種相。一、有欲樂，二、無偏黨，三、除匱乏，四、具正智。
items.en: Further, an almsgiver has four marks. First, having genuine aspiration; second, being free of favoritism; third, relieving want; fourth, possessing correct understanding.

items.title: The Four Marks of a Genuine Precept-Holder

items.zh: 具尸羅者亦有四相。一、有欲樂，二、結橋梁，三、不現行，四、具正智。
items.en: One who upholds moral discipline likewise has four marks. First, having genuine aspiration; second, forming a bridge; third, non-manifestation; fourth, possessing correct understanding.

items.title: The Four Marks of a Genuine Meditator

items.zh: 成就修者亦有四相。一、欲解清淨，二、引攝清淨，三、勝解定清淨，四、智清淨。又
items.en: One who accomplishes meditative cultivation likewise has four marks. First, purity of aspiration and understanding; second, purity of what is drawn in; third, purity of resolved concentration; fourth, purity of wisdom.

items.title: The Six Kinds of Recipients of Alms

items.zh: 受施者有六種。一、受學受施，二、活命受施，三、貧匱受施，四、棄捨受施，五、羈遊受施，六、耽著受施。
items.en: Further, recipients of alms are of six kinds. First, receiving for the sake of learning; second, receiving to sustain life; third, receiving out of poverty and want; fourth, receiving what has been relinquished; fifth, receiving while travelling and lodging away from home; sixth, receiving out of attachment.

items.title: Eight Kinds of Harm a Compassionate Mind Should Recognise

items.zh: 復有八種損惱。一、飢損惱，二、渴損惱，三、麁食損惱，四、疲倦損惱，五、寒損惱，六、熱損惱，七、無覆障損惱，八、有覆障損惱。
items.en: There are, further, eight kinds of harm. First, harm from hunger; second, harm from thirst; third, harm from coarse food; fourth, harm from exhaustion; fifth, harm from cold; sixth, harm from heat; seventh, harm from lacking shelter; eighth, harm from being shut off from light.

items.zh: 復有六種損惱。一、俱生，二、所欲匱乏，三、逼切，四、時節變異，五、流漏，六、事業休廢。
items.en: There are, further, six kinds of harm, gathering the same eight into fewer categories: first, that which is innate; second, want of what is desired; third, that which presses and constrains; fourth, seasonal change; fifth, exposure; sixth, the cessation of activity.

items.title: Six Ways to Actually Benefit Someone in Distress

items.zh: 復有六種攝益：一、任持攝益，二、勇健無損攝益，三、覆護攝益，四、塗香攝益，五、衣服攝益，六、共住攝益。
items.en: There are, further, six kinds of benefit. First, the benefit of sustenance; second, the benefit of vigour without harm; third, the benefit of shelter; fourth, the benefit of fragrant ointment; fifth, the benefit of clothing; sixth, the benefit of communal dwelling.

items.title: Four Marks of a Poor Companion, and Four Marks of a Good One

items.zh: 復有四種非善友相。一、不捨怨心，二、引彼不愛，三、遮彼所愛，四、引非所宜。與此相違，當知即是四善友相。
items.en: There are, further, four marks of one who is not a good companion. First, not letting go of resentment; second, bringing about what is disliked; third, obstructing what is liked; fourth, leading towards what is unsuitable. The reverse of these should be understood as the four marks of a good companion.

items.title: Three Things Practice Draws a Person Towards, and Four Kinds of Attending on Others

items.zh: 復有三種引攝。一、引攝資生具，二、引攝有喜樂，三、引攝離喜樂。復有四種隨轉供事。一、隨轉供事非知舊者，二、隨轉供事諸親友者，三、隨轉供事所尊重者，四、隨轉供事具福慧者。
items.en: There are, further, three things drawn towards: first, being drawn towards life's supporting requisites; second, being drawn towards states possessing joy and bliss; third, being drawn towards states free of joy and bliss. There are, further, four ways of attending on and serving others: first, attending on one who is not a prior acquaintance; second, attending on one's own relatives and friends; third, attending on one whom one respects; fourth, attending on one endowed with merit and wisdom.

items.zh: 由此四種隨轉供事，依止四處，獲得五果應知。何等四處？一、無攝受處，二、無侵惱處，三、應供養處，四、同分隨轉處。依此四處，能感五果：一、感大財富，二、名稱普聞，三、離諸煩惱，四、證得涅槃，五、或往善趣。
items.en: Through these four ways of attending on and serving others, resting on four grounds, five results are obtained, as should be understood. What are the four grounds? First, the ground of no prior connection; second, the ground of mutual harmlessness; third, the ground worthy of offering; fourth, the ground of shared practice. Resting on these four grounds, five results are brought about: first, great wealth; second, widespread renown; third, freedom from every affliction; fourth, the realisation of nirvāṇa; fifth, or else a favourable rebirth.

items.title: The Three Wisdoms, the Three Trainings, and Sound Reasoning Attention Concludes

items.zh: 又聰慧者有三種聰慧相。一、於善受行，二、於善決定，三、於善堅固。復有三相。一、受學增上戒，二、受學增上心，三、受學增上慧。
items.en: Further, one who is truly wise has three marks of wisdom: first, faithfully carrying out what is wholesome; second, being resolved in what is wholesome; third, being steadfast in what is wholesome. There are, further, three marks: first, training in heightened moral discipline; second, training in a heightened mind; third, training in heightened wisdom.

blocks.text: The last reading of fascicle 5, and of our first phase (fascicles 1–5). After so much analysis, the treatise ends the section on sound reasoning attention with practical ethics: how to earn and use wealth, how to give, keep precepts, and meditate, how to help those in distress, and how to recognise a good companion. It is a fitting close: understanding is meant to show in conduct.

Sound reasoning attention in seeking means pursuing wealth "by lawful and non-violent means" (不凶險). Both teachers read 凶險 more broadly than violence: blameworthy and ill-omened, as when money is made by fraud. In enjoying wealth it means using it "without being bound by it", neither hoarding nor squandering, sharing it with others, and seeing its dangers.

Correct conduct includes honouring parents and elders, fearing wrongdoing, giving, making merit, and "observing fasting and upholding the precepts" (受齋持戒). Venerable Miào Jìng distinguishes the two: 受齋 is a lay follower's short-term practice of monastic discipline, such as the eight precepts on observance days; 持戒 is lifelong.
The provisions for the three vehicles are promised "in full" later, in the stages of the hearers, solitary realisers, and bodhisattvas. Here the treatise gives an outline.
A true giver has genuine aspiration, no favouritism, relieves want, and has correct understanding. Master Cháng Bǎi: "The wise do not cling to their giving."

A precept-holder takes the precepts sincerely; makes them "a bridge" (Venerable Miào Jìng: the lower realms are a river, and keeping precepts crosses it); keeps them without display ("not manifesting outwardly"; Venerable Miào Jìng adds a second reading, not losing mindfulness through affliction); and keeps them purely.

A meditator's practice is pure in four ways. Master Cháng Bǎi sets the bar: to speak of "cultivation" (修) one needs at least **access concentration**. Venerable Miào Jìng repeats the order of Day 19: giving is easier, precepts harder, meditation hardest.
Six ways of receiving alms are listed, including "receiving what has been relinquished": the rag robes stitched from cloth others had thrown away.

A compassionate mind should recognise eight kinds of harm (from hunger and thirst to being "shut off from light", which the *Pīxún jì* reads as failing eyes and another commentary as imprisonment), and six ways of benefiting someone in distress. Master Cháng Bǎi's modern example of "the benefit of fragrant ointment": giving fans or air-conditioning so monastics can practise in the heat.

A poor companion does not let go of resentment, among other marks; a good one does. Master Cháng Bǎi's example: Subhūti, dwelling in the samādhi of non-contention, knew that some people grew angry at the sight of him, so on such days he skipped his alms round rather than provoke them.

Sound reasoning attention draws one towards meditative absorptions and towards liberation; it is completed in the three wisdoms (from hearing, reflection, and cultivation) and the three **heightened trainings** in discipline, mind, and wisdom. Both teachers: 增上 ("heightened") means both "leading higher" and "unsurpassed", not shared with non-Buddhists, whose discipline and concentration do not lead beyond the three realms.

We have now read the first five fascicles: the stage of the five senses, the Mind Stage, and the first half of the three grounds of thought. The arc has gone from a moment of seeing, through death and rebirth, the world's formation, the classification of everything, and the survey of the three realms, to causation, and finally to right attention and ethical life. Fascicle 6 continues the three grounds with "what does not accord with reason": sixteen mistaken views, beginning with the view that the result already exists in the cause.

quiz.q: Sound seeking pursues wealth "by lawful and non-凶險 means," rendered "non-violent." How do the teachers read 凶險?
options: blameworthy and inauspicious — e.g., earning money by fraud is a wrong, hence 凶險
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "Making money by deceit and fraud is a wrong — that is what 凶險 means." Venerable Miào Jìng: "凶險 means blameworthy; where there is wrongdoing there is ill omen"; Buddhists obey both the law of the land and the precepts. "Violent" is narrower — fraud is not violent, yet it is 凶險.

quiz.q: Correct conduct includes 受齋持戒, rendered "observes fasting, and upholds the precepts." According to Venerable Miào Jìng, how do 受齋 and 持戒 differ?
options: 受齋 is a lay follower's short-term practice of monastic virtue, such as the eight precepts; 持戒 is long-term
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "受齋 means training in discipline, concentration, and wisdom — lay followers practising monastic virtues"; "持戒 is long-term; 受齋 includes precepts too, but short-term." He adds that going to the office while keeping the eight precepts "is not quite proper." "Fasting" captures only one side of 齋.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, what are an almsgiver's four marks?
options: genuine aspiration, no favoritism, relieving want, correct understanding
quiz.why: "First, having genuine aspiration; second, being free of favoritism; third, relieving want; fourth, possessing correct understanding." Master Cháng Bǎi: "The wise do not cling to their giving — the three spheres are empty; that is correct understanding." Venerable Miào Jìng: giving without believing in cause and effect is not correct understanding. C and D belong to the meditator and the precept-holder.

quiz.q: The precept-holder's second mark is "forming a bridge." How does Venerable Miào Jìng explain it?
options: the lower realms are like a river; keeping precepts is crossing it by a bridge
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "Say the three lower realms are a river: by keeping precepts I pass beyond them, as if crossing the river on a bridge." A is literal merit-work, not the sense here.

quiz.q: The accomplished meditator has four purities. According to Master Cháng Bǎi, what level is needed to call it "cultivation" (修)?
options: at least access concentration or above
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "To speak of cultivation, one needs at least access concentration." Venerable Miào Jìng: giving is easier, precepts harder, meditation harder still; "resolve" is really insight and "concentration" is calm. (The reading note says he maps all four purities onto the four dhyānas one by one; the lecture does not — logged in the correction list.)

quiz.q: The first mark of a poor companion is "not letting go of resentment." What does Master Cháng Bǎi say Subhūti did, as a model of a good companion?
options: knowing some people grew angry at the sight of him, he skipped his alms round that day so as not to provoke them
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: Subhūti, dwelling in the samādhi of non-contention, "knowing some would grow angry seeing him, did not go for alms that day so as not to anger them"; also, "monastics hold no grudge overnight — once things are cleared up, no resentment remains." Venerable Miào Jìng: first anger is understandable, "but by the second thought one should let it go." (The reading note says he merely skipped one household; the lecture says he skipped the whole alms round — logged in the correction list.)

quiz.q: The wise train in heightened discipline, mind, and wisdom. According to the teachers, what two senses does 增上 (heightened) have?
options: "leading towards" — taking one higher; "most excellent" — not shared with non-Buddhists, whose discipline, concentration, and wisdom are not "heightened"
rising to heaven or the form realm
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "增上 has two senses: 'leading towards' — going somewhere higher; and 'most excellent' — not shared with non-Buddhists"; "non-Buddhists also have discipline, concentration, and wisdom, but not heightened ones — theirs carry wrong views." Venerable Miào Jìng cites the same two readings. The section's first three marks: carrying out the good (learning-wisdom), being resolved in it, and being steadfast in it.
